concepts.title: Market Equilibrium: Equilibrium Price and Quantity
concepts.definition: A competitive market is in equilibrium where the quantity all buyers plan to purchase equals the quantity all firms plan to sell, so the market clears; for straight-line demand and supply curves the clearing price is found by solving the two equations together.
concepts.key_idea: One price reconciles the plans of every buyer and seller, and the quantity traded there is the equilibrium quantity.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1 and 5.1.1, Example 5.1 wheat market, pages 72-74
question_patterns: define the situation where quantity bought equals quantity sold and the market clears
solve for the clearing price and quantity from linear demand and supply equations

solution_steps.action: Take the gap between the curve intercepts
solution_steps.explain: Writing demand as a minus b times p and supply as c plus d times p, the intercept gap drives the solution.
The slopes of demand and supply together scale the intercept gap.
Setting demand equal to supply and solving gives the equilibrium price as the gap over the slope sum.
Substituting the clearing price into either curve gives the equilibrium quantity exchanged.

worked_examples.question: Using Market Equilibrium: Equilibrium Price and Quantity, compute the result for demand_intercept = 3, supply_intercept = 3, demand_slope = 3, supply_slope = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the gap between the curve intercepts: price_gap = demand_intercept - supply_intercept = 0.0 Step 2: Add the two slopes: slope_sum = demand_slope + supply_slope = 5.0 Step 3: Solve for the clearing price: equilibrium_price = price_gap / slope_sum = 0.0 Step 4: Read off the traded quantity: equilibrium_quantity = demand_intercept - demand_slope * equilibrium_price = 3.0 Final result: 3.0

worked_examples.question: Using Market Equilibrium: Equilibrium Price and Quantity, compute the result for demand_intercept = 4, supply_intercept = 4, demand_slope = 4, supply_slope = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the gap between the curve intercepts: price_gap = demand_intercept - supply_intercept = 0.0 Step 2: Add the two slopes: slope_sum = demand_slope + supply_slope = 7.0 Step 3: Solve for the clearing price: equilibrium_price = price_gap / slope_sum = 0.0 Step 4: Read off the traded quantity: equilibrium_quantity = demand_intercept - demand_slope * equilibrium_price = 4.0 Final result: 4.0

concepts.title: Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment
concepts.definition: At any price below the clearing level buyers want more than sellers offer - excess demand - and price is bid up; above it sellers offer more than buyers take - excess supply - and price is cut, the invisible hand pushing the market back to equilibrium.
concepts.key_idea: Shortages raise price, gluts lower it, and the drift stops only where the market clears.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1, out-of-equilibrium behaviour and Example 5.1 algebra, pages 72-74
question_patterns: explain the rule that shortages push the price up and gluts push it down until the market clears

solution_steps.explain: Subtracting quantity supplied from quantity demanded at the going price gives the market imbalance; a positive value is excess demand, a negative one excess supply.
Positive imbalance pushes the price up, negative imbalance pulls it down, and the movement halts at the clearing price.

concepts.title: Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour
concepts.definition: Firms hire labour until the wage equals the marginal revenue product of labour - the extra revenue from one more worker - which under price taking equals price times marginal product; households weigh income against leisure, giving an upward-sloping market supply of labour, and the wage settles where the two curves cross.
concepts.key_idea: Hiring stops where the last worker adds exactly what the wage costs, and that rule slopes labour demand downward.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1.1, wage determination in labour market box, pages 75-77
question_patterns: compute the revenue value of an extra worker from price and marginal product

solution_steps.action: Value the extra output of a worker
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the marginal product of labour by the revenue earned per unit of output to get the marginal revenue product.
The firm keeps hiring while the revenue product exceeds the wage and stops at equality, which is the labour demand rule.

worked_examples.question: Using Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour, compute the result for marginal_revenue = 3, marginal_product_of_labour = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Value the extra output of a worker: marginal_revenue_product_of_labour = marginal_revenue * marginal_product_of_labour = 9.0 Final result: 9.0

worked_examples.question: Using Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour, compute the result for marginal_revenue = 4, marginal_product_of_labour = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Value the extra output of a worker: marginal_revenue_product_of_labour = marginal_revenue * marginal_product_of_labour = 16.0 Final result: 16.0

concepts.title: Effects of a Demand Shift on Equilibrium
concepts.definition: With the number of firms fixed, a rightward shift of demand - from higher incomes for a normal good or more buyers - raises both equilibrium price and quantity, while a leftward shift lowers both; price and quantity always move together when demand shifts.
concepts.formula: demand_shift_right implies price_up and quantity_up (supply unchanged)
concepts.key_idea: Move demand and equilibrium slides along the supply curve, carrying price and quantity in the same direction.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1.1, demand shift discussion and figure 5.2, pages 77-78
question_patterns: how do equilibrium price and quantity respond when consumer income rises for a normal good

show the new equilibrium after demand falls, using a diagram
does an income rise affect the supply curve of the good

solution_steps.action: Identify the shift and its cause
solution_steps.explain: Income growth for a normal good or an inflow of buyers shifts demand rightward; the reverses shift it leftward.

solution_steps.action: Register the imbalance at the old price
solution_steps.explain: A rightward shift creates excess demand at the old price, so price is bid up; a leftward shift creates excess supply and price falls.
Moving along the unchanged supply curve, both price and quantity rise after a rightward shift and fall after a leftward one.

concepts.title: Effects of a Supply Shift on Equilibrium
concepts.definition: With demand unchanged, a leftward supply shift - say from costlier inputs - raises equilibrium price and lowers quantity, while a rightward supply shift from better technology or more firms lowers price and raises quantity; price and quantity move in opposite directions when supply shifts.
concepts.formula: supply_shift_left implies price_up and quantity_down (demand unchanged)
concepts.key_idea: Move supply and equilibrium slides along the demand curve, pushing price and quantity in opposite directions.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1.1, supply shift discussion and figure 5.3, pages 79-80
question_patterns: how do equilibrium price and quantity respond when an input becomes dearer

solution_steps.action: Identify the shift and its cause
solution_steps.explain: Costlier inputs shift supply leftward; better technology or more firms shift it rightward, leaving demand untouched.

solution_steps.action: Register the imbalance at the old price
solution_steps.explain: A leftward shift creates excess demand at the old price and price rises; a rightward shift creates excess supply and price falls.
Moving along the unchanged demand curve, price rises while quantity falls after a leftward shift, and the reverse after a rightward one.

concepts.title: Simultaneous Shifts of Demand and Supply
concepts.definition: When both curves move at once, one equilibrium variable is pinned down by the direction of the shifts and the other depends on their relative size: same-direction shifts fix quantity but leave price ambiguous, opposite-direction shifts fix price but leave quantity ambiguous.
concepts.formula: both_shift_right implies quantity_up; price_ambiguous (depends on magnitudes)
concepts.key_idea: A shift fixes its own variable - demand governs quantity direction, supply governs price direction - and magnitudes settle the rest.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1.1, simultaneous shifts and Table 5.1, pages 80-81
question_patterns: what happens to price and quantity when demand and supply both shift rightward

solution_steps.explain: Note whether each curve moves rightward or leftward to place the case in the four-way table.
Same-direction shifts settle quantity - up for twin rightward, down for twin leftward; opposite-direction shifts settle price - up when demand rises or supply falls relative to the other.
The remaining variable can rise, fall or stay put depending on which shift is larger, so only magnitudes can decide it.

concepts.title: Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms
concepts.definition: With identical firms free to enter or leave, supernormal profits attract entrants and losses drive exits until price settles at the minimum average cost; the equilibrium quantity is whatever demand absorbs at that price, and the number of firms is that quantity divided by each firm's output.
concepts.key_idea: Entry and exit police profits to normal, pinning price at the average cost floor while quantity follows demand.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.1.2, Example 5.2 wheat market with entry, pages 81-84
question_patterns: why must the long run price equal the minimum average cost under free entry and exit
compute the number of firms in equilibrium from total quantity and per firm output

wheat demand is 200 minus p and each firm supplies 10 plus p above price 20, find the market outcome

solution_steps.action: Set the price at the cost floor
solution_steps.explain: Free entry and exit force price to the minimum average cost of the identical firms.
Substituting that price into the market demand curve gives the equilibrium quantity.
Each identical firm produces its share at that price, so dividing total quantity by the per-firm output gives the number of firms.

worked_examples.question: Using Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms, compute the result for minimum_average_cost = 3, demand_intercept = 3, demand_slope = 3, output_per_firm = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Set the price at the cost floor: equilibrium_price = minimum_average_cost = 3.0 Step 2: Let demand set total output: equilibrium_quantity = demand_intercept - demand_slope * equilibrium_price = -6.0 Step 3: Divide the market among firms: number_of_firms = equilibrium_quantity / output_per_firm = -3.0 Final result: -3.0

worked_examples.question: Using Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms, compute the result for minimum_average_cost = 4, demand_intercept = 4, demand_slope = 4, output_per_firm = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Set the price at the cost floor: equilibrium_price = minimum_average_cost = 4.0 Step 2: Let demand set total output: equilibrium_quantity = demand_intercept - demand_slope * equilibrium_price = -12.0 Step 3: Divide the market among firms: number_of_firms = equilibrium_quantity / output_per_firm = -4.0 Final result: -4.0

concepts.title: Price Ceiling and Rationing
concepts.definition: A price ceiling is a government-imposed maximum set below the market clearing price for essentials; it creates a shortage that is usually shared out by rationing through fair price shops, bringing long queues and the risk of a black market.
concepts.key_idea: Capping the price below equilibrium makes goods cheaper but scarcer, so rationing must ration out the shortfall.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.2.1, figure 5.7 and consequences, pages 84-85
question_patterns: what is a price ceiling and why is it set below the equilibrium price
compute the shortage created when a maximum price is imposed on a good

solution_steps.action: Compare the ceiling with the clearing price
solution_steps.explain: A ceiling binds only when it sits below the market clearing price.
At the ceiling price buyers demand more than firms supply, producing an excess demand or shortage.
Ration coupons and fair price shops share the limited supply, but queues and black market premiums typically follow.

concepts.title: Price Floor and Support Programmes
concepts.definition: A price floor is a government-imposed minimum set above the market clearing price, as in farm support prices or minimum wage laws; it creates a surplus that the government must buy up, or in the labour market, potential unemployment.
concepts.key_idea: Propping the price above equilibrium rewards sellers per unit but leaves unsold surplus for the state to absorb.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec205.txt, section 5.2.2, figure 5.8 and examples, pages 85-86
question_patterns: what is a price floor and why is it set above the equilibrium price

solution_steps.action: Compare the floor with the clearing price
solution_steps.explain: A floor binds only when it sits above the market clearing price.
At the floor price firms offer more than buyers take, producing an excess supply or surplus.
In farm support schemes the government purchases the surplus at the assured price; a minimum wage leaves some job seekers without work at the legislated wage.
